title: Lithium scale-making and extractivist counter-futurities in Bolivia
abstract: of lithium industrialization in Bolivia to contribute to wider debates - in anthropology and beyond - about the essentially contested nature of the green energy transition. Based on research conducted between 2019 and 2023, the article examines the topographies of production and sociopolitical mobilization that are entangled with Bolivia's state-controlled lithium project but which resist the various pressures to reorient social and productive worlds around arguably the most important 'critical' mineral for climate policy-making. The article develops a theoretical framework for understanding these localized counter-futurities, one in which the image of scale-making takes on both vertical and horizontal dimensions. An anthropology of energy, climate justice, and resource imaginaries that is critically attuned to these inter-scalar frictions is one that must also be able to project itself through the kaleidoscope of competing energy narratives as a form of both demystification and ethnographic truth-telling.
title_zh: 玻利维亚的锂尺度制造与榨取主义反未来
abstract_zh: 本文通过玻利维亚锂工业化案例，为人类学及其他领域关于绿色能源转型本质争议性的更广泛辩论做出贡献。基于2019年至2023年间进行的研究，本文考察了与玻利维亚国家控制锂项目纠缠在一起的生产地形和社会政治动员，但抵制了围绕对气候政策制定而言最重要的“关键”矿物来重新定位社会和世界各种压力。本文发展了一个理论框架来理解这些地方性的反未来，其中尺度制造的图像同时具有垂直和水平维度。一个对能源、气候正义和资源想象进行人类学研究，并批判性地关注这些跨尺度摩擦的领域，也必须能够通过竞争性能源叙事的万花筒来投射自身，作为一种去神秘化和民族志真相讲述的形式。

title: Mapping the structure and dynamics of global high‐tech aerospace trade
journal_name: GLOBAL NETWORKS-A JOURNAL OF TRANSNATIONAL AFFAIRS
abstract: Abstract The aerospace industry is a fast‐growing high‐tech sector related to the national economic lifeline and national defence security. In the context of prosperous cooperation and fierce competition between countries, a multi‐layered global aerospace network, from production to trade, has been formed. However, the high‐tech aerospace trade structure and its spatial pattern as the mirror of the industry lack systematic research. This study constructs global high‐tech aerospace trade networks to review the trade dynamics, identify the core countries and explore the regional structure and geographical characteristics. Different high‐tech aerospace segments show varying evolutionary characteristics, with exports more concentrated than imports. The United States and Western Europe dominate the import and export market in all categories of high‐tech aerospace trade, especially in high‐end segment, holding organizational authority in the community structure. Although Asia is rising rapidly in some areas, it still has a long way to go to become a global hub.
title_zh: 全球高科技航空航天贸易结构与动态图谱
abstract_zh: 航空航天工业是一个快速增长的高科技行业，关系到国家经济命脉和国防安全。在国家间合作繁荣与竞争激烈的背景下，一个从生产到贸易的多层次全球航空航天网络已经形成。然而，作为行业镜像的高科技航空航天贸易结构及其空间格局缺乏系统性研究。本研究构建了全球高科技航空航天贸易网络，以审视贸易动态、识别核心国家并探究区域结构和地理特征。不同高科技航空航天细分领域显示出不同的演化特征，出口比进口更加集中。美国和西欧在所有类别的高科技航空航天贸易中主导进出口市场，尤其在高端的细分领域，并在社区结构中拥有组织权威。尽管亚洲在某些领域迅速崛起，但要成为全球枢纽仍有很长的路要走。

title: Mining the Energy Transition: An Introduction
abstract: Mining the Energy Transition:An Introduction Angela Kronenburg García and Nikkie Wiegink In 2018, when one of the authors of this article (Angela) was doing field-work in northern Mozambique—a country of research interest to both authors—she ended up following a series of public consultations announcing a new mining project in the area. These consultations were organized by the mining company in the district's town and in the various villages that would be affected and resettled by the project. Angela was primarily interested in the topic of investor-induced displacement—the fact that the investor was a mining company was a coincidence. She actually knew very little about the resource that was going to be mined (graphite) and what it is used for. During the consultation meetings the project was presented to local residents with the help of visual materials (posters, slides). One of the slides was titled, "For what reason is graphite important?" and displayed a photo of an electric car and a solar farm. It explained that graphite was a critical component for these "green technologies" and that there was a growing market for graphite. These concerns were far removed from the lives and realities of local residents and, as a result, this information largely went unnoticed. Instead, the discussions during the public consultations were dominated by people's hopes for jobs and worries about displacement and the loss of agricultural land because of the multiple graphite mines popping up in the region (Wiegink and Kronenburg García 2022). The global connections of what was happening in this mining area in Mozambique only started to dawn on Angela when, in the Netherlands and Belgium, after a period of time, she started to observe electric vehicles charging on the streets and noticed the inescapable talk [End Page 311] about an energy transition on the news. This was in stark contrast with the Mozambican context, where "the energy transition" was not yet part of the public debate (Warner et al. 2023). There, discussions about the energy transition came later, haltingly at first, and only started to take off around 2021, initially through donor-government interactions and later in national policy circles. A few years later, in September 2023, the first-ever Africa Climate Summit took place in Nairobi, Kenya. The Summit was a high-profile event, bringing together African heads of state and other leaders such as United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen and United States Special Presidential Envoy for Climate John Kerry, as well as policymakers, development partners, the private sector and civil society organizations. The aim of the summit was to deliberate on solutions for climate change in Africa and agree on a common African position ahead of the 28th meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP28) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. One of the main topics discussed was Africa's contribution to the global energy transition. Under a "green growth" agenda that called for more climate investments in Africa, energy transition plans and strategies were presented (including by the Mozambican delegation), highlighting the continent's untapped "renewable energy" potential and its abundant reserves of "green minerals." The latter feeds into the strategic quest of the European Union (EU) and the US to secure "critical raw materials" for low-carbon technologies. The Africa Climate Summit not only indicates that the energy transition has now truly gone global but also signals a further entrenchment and legitimization of a new "green" extractive rush, such as the one happening for graphite in northern Mozambique. Taken together, these examples illustrate two important characteristics of the energy transition that we would like to foreground in this introduction. First, that the energy transition, with its associated notions of "greenness," has become a dominant narrative that is increasingly doing all sorts of things in the world. We believe this may indicate a "moment of energopolitical change" generating "fissures and tremors" (Boyer 2014:315) across the globe that merit serious anthropological attention. Second, the energy transition is intimately connected to resource extraction, to the extent that many of these fissures and tremors are materializing and reverberating in...
title_zh: 开采能源转型：引言
abstract_zh: 《开采能源转型：引言》安吉拉·克罗嫩堡·加西亚和尼基·维金克。2018年，当本文作者之一（安吉拉）在莫桑比克北部进行田野调查时——这是一个两位作者都感兴趣的研究国家——她最终参与了一系列公开咨询会，宣布该地区的一个新采矿项目。这些咨询会由采矿公司在地区城镇和各个将受项目影响并搬迁的村庄组织。安吉拉主要对投资者引发的搬迁感兴趣；投资者是采矿公司纯属巧合。她实际上对所开采的资源（石墨）及其用途知之甚少。在咨询会上，项目通过视觉材料（海报、幻灯片）向当地居民展示。一张幻灯片标题为“石墨为何重要？”，并展示了电动汽车和太阳能农场的照片。它解释说石墨是这些“绿色技术”的关键组成部分，并且石墨市场正在增长。这些关切与当地居民的生活和现实相去甚远，因此这些信息基本上被忽视。相反，公开咨询会上的讨论主要围绕人们对就业的希望以及对搬迁和失去农业土地的担忧，因为该地区出现了多个石墨矿（Wiegink and Kronenburg García 2022）。安吉拉直到后来在荷兰和比利时，看到街上充电的电动汽车并注意到新闻中关于能源转型的不可避免的讨论时，才开始意识到莫桑比克这个矿区所发生事情的全球联系。这与莫桑比克的情况形成鲜明对比，在那里“能源转型”尚未成为公共辩论的一部分（Warner et al. 2023）。在那里，关于能源转型的讨论来得较晚，起初断断续续，直到2021年左右才开始通过捐助者-政府互动以及后来的国家政策圈子兴起。几年后，2023年9月，首届非洲气候峰会在肯尼亚内罗毕举行。这是一场高规格活动，汇聚了非洲国家元首和其他领导人，如联合国秘书长安东尼奥·古特雷斯、欧盟委员会主席乌尔苏拉·冯德莱恩和美国总统气候特使约翰·克里，以及政策制定者、发展伙伴、私营部门和民间社会组织。峰会旨在商讨非洲气候变化的解决方案，并在联合国气候变化框架公约第28次缔约方会议（COP28）之前达成一个共同的非洲立场。讨论的主要议题之一是非洲对全球能源转型的贡献。在呼吁更多气候投资的“绿色增长”议程下，提出了能源转型计划和战略（包括莫桑比克代表团的发言），强调了非洲大陆未开发的“可再生能源”潜力及其丰富的“绿色矿产”储量。后者迎合了欧盟和美国确保低碳技术“关键原材料”的战略追求。非洲气候峰会不仅表明能源转型现已真正全球化，也标志着一种新的“绿色”采掘热潮的进一步巩固和合法化，例如莫桑比克北部的石墨热潮。综合来看，这些例子说明了能源转型的两个重要特征，我们想在此引言中着重强调。首先，能源转型及其相关的“绿色”概念已成为一种主导叙事，并在世界上发挥着越来越大的作用。我们认为这可能表明一个“能量政治变化的时刻”，在全球范围内产生“裂缝和震动”（Boyer 2014:315），值得严肃的人类学关注。其次，能源转型与资源开采密切相关，以至于许多这些裂缝和震动正在物质化并在...中回响。

title: Nuclear ghost: Atomic livelihoods in Fukushima's Gray Zone By RyoMorimoto, Oakland, CA: University of California Press. 2023. 339 pp.
abstract: What do you do with knowledge? Ryo Morimoto's ethnography of post-3.11 Fukushima, Japan, and the lifeways of residents who choose to stay despite the ongoing damage caused by the earthquake, tsunami, and nuclear disaster at the Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO)’s nuclear power plant, focuses on Minamisōma, a “supposedly unremarkable place with [a] hypervisualized threat of radiation” (245). Wielding his Geiger counter, Morimoto offers the reading to Hatsumi, the elderly woman whose acerbic, wise, and weary insights orient his analysis. “What do you do with the knowledge of [your Geiger counter]?” Hatsumi angrily asks him (16). In what way would a seemingly “objective” measure of something invisible be mobilized, used, with what intentions and consequences? Morimoto's initial desire to document the harms done to communities as collateral damage of Japan's nuclear complex, structured by the inequalities of rural-urban divides in which the hinterlands sacrifice for the production of Tokyo's electricity, bumped up against Hatsumi's query. And if numerical measures of radiation might be used, so might ethnographic research. There are hazards in replicating damage-centered public discourses. What story should the ethnographer of post-3.11 Japan tells? What are the stakes of scientific knowledge production more broadly, including ethnographic knowledge that parses “shapeshifting science, politics, laws, and media reports” (239)? The “nuclear ghost” of Morimoto's title is a concept offered by Hatsumi early in his research and, like his early fieldwork realizations that he was looking at the wrong things for the wrong reasons, reappears throughout the text. The nuclear ghost encapsulates the experience of post-3.11 Japan in which something invisible and scary becomes hyper-visualized (through public representations, radiation monitoring stations, plastic bags filled with contaminated soil, Morimoto's own Geiger counter), eclipsing the people, lifeways, and stories that, Morimoto argues, are the proper object of attention. However, we should not disregard radiation's dangers. For many of Morimoto's interlocutors, living with radiation in one's home, cultivating the soil that generations have cultivated, is the condition of living a meaningful life and dying a good death. Ecologically interlinked webs of en—ineffable connections—emplace people and their relationships in context. Detangling the often-contradictory science-in-development surrounding radiation exposure and decontamination, Morimoto shows how “reasonable” exposure means different things to different people, and well-being must be understood holistically. Fukushima's “gray zone” refers to both geographical spaces marked by shifting evacuation zone designations (Chapter 3), with equally shifting policies that determine compensation for residents (Chapter 4), and the epistemological indeterminacies surrounding radiation's short- and long-term impacts. Political decisions (that led, rather than followed, scientific determinations) produced the “divided community” of Minamisōma, where “contaminants fell unevenly on top of preexisting social, cultural, and political boundaries, which residents continuously lived within and used to reorient themselves to the post-3.11 world” (52). Reorientations toward the topic of radiation were strategic, pragmatic, and existential. In one key passage (137), Morimoto describes how from the perspective of people holding antinuclear or antigovernmental political positions, “the TEPCO accident had to remain dangerous”; other people had stakes in maintaining specific levels of governmental compensation for lost and damaged property, so “the contamination from the TEPCO accident had to be deemed unsafe.” For others, like Morimoto's elderly interlocutors who hoped to return home to “die well,” “the persistent presence of contaminants and the associated compensation were signs of an extended period of alienation that needed to end” (137). Different actors needed different things from social and scientific consensus, though consensus was not to be found. In its absence, the question was, indeed, what to do—is it safe to go home?—and how desires, in addition to damage, oriented people's actions. In this context, Morimoto's book explores “the limits of science as the dominant approach to confronting an invisible hazard in society” (137), an orientation familiar to many in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. This is a hefty ethnography, and I could imagine teaching chapters in undergraduate and graduate seminars in medical anthropology, environmental anthropology, science and technology studies, and Japanese studies. My favorite chapters were the more tightly focused. For instance, Chapter 5, “Radioactive Mosquitoes and the Science of Half-Lives,” juxtaposes Morimoto's participation in Radiation Safety Officer training at Columbia University with a radiation-focused radio show in Fukushima by a scientist called Dr. Tsubokura. The theme for Safety Officer training was to keep radiation exposure “as low as reasonably achievable” (123), while simultaneously, public concern about radiation was represented as “unscientific” and “phobia-driven” (124). In contrast, Dr. Tsubokura understood people's desire for locally specific data. By accounting for local ecologies and social networks, he gave nuanced attention to how residents might make informed risk-reduction decisions. Morimoto's own message aligns with that of Dr. Tsubokura: while radiation is indeed harmful, there are other potentially more devastating harms—like secondary health risks of evacuation—that neither the state nor public discourses about the TEPCO accident sufficiently attend to. These other risks could have been discussed in more detail in the book, and one has the impression that the elision of residents’ narratives is, from the ethnographer's perspective, as devastating as any health impact. Another fantastic chapter, Chapter 9, “A Wild Boar Chase,” focuses on state inattention to ecological context in remediation strategies. It turns out that the Japanese government had been chasing wild boars away from exclusion zones, without considering where the boars went. This chapter beautifully and tragically elaborates how “decontamination has produced an ecology of harm in coastal Fukushima that has rendered locals, wild boars, local food chains, and the land itself complicit in the production of nuclear waste” (216). Boars—which happily inhabit land disturbed by human cultivation, eat the delicious foods humans normally forage, and are normally a human food source—were now hunted only to be incinerated as nuclear waste. This book “about” post-3.11 Fukushima is relevant to topics far beyond. There are many resonances in Morimoto's findings with my own recent work connected to a devastating local fire in the wildland-urban interface of Boulder County, Colorado—in the community divisions regarding who is considered a legitimate “sufferer” (4) and whether it is worse to lose one's home, or have one's home intact but indeterminately contaminated (50). My collaborations with atmospheric scientists on often invisible air pollution made knowable through technoscientific measurements speak to the same complicated relationships between quantifiable data and subjective experiences that Morimoto tracks, in which quantitative “data do not necessarily validate or speak to individuals’ subjective experiences, and, at times, the data might deny them” (134). Morimoto's book presses us to consider anew the role of visibility and invisibility in perceiving and knowing. Technoscientific advances have long made visible otherwise imperceptible phenomena. Is the “nuclear ghost” truly scarier because radiation is invisible (114)? What is intangible is also easier to ignore, and distance enables the illusion of safety. As with other forms of energy generation, “[n]uclear power is a social technology that produces and reproduces a community of the exposable,” and Morimoto reminds us that “public and political discourse [should] pay attention to individual stories and local histories behind exposure” (237). In the North American context, the concept of an environmental justice community might be a double-edged sword, as damage-centered narratives elide the complicated attachments people may feel to their land and even to polluting industries, often a source of livelihood. While highlighting intersectional and disproportionate harms, the concept also cordons off those communities from the rest. There is power in arguing, as Morimoto does, that “[w]e have all been living in the same radioactive world” (234). The stakes belong to all of us.
title_zh: 核幽灵：福岛灰色地带中的原子生计
abstract_zh: 你用知识做什么？Ryo Morimoto对日本3.11后福岛的民族志研究，以及那些选择留在遭受地震、海啸和东京电力公司（TEPCO）核电站核灾难持续破坏的居民的生活方式，聚焦于南相马——一个“辐射威胁被超视觉化的看似平凡之地”（245页）。Morimoto手持盖革计数器，向Hatsumi这位老妇人朗读读数，她尖刻、明智而疲惫的见解引导着他的分析。“你知道你的盖革计数器在做什么吗？”Hatsumi愤怒地质问他（16页）。一个看似“客观”的对无形之物的测量，会以何种方式被动员、使用，带着何种意图和后果？Morimoto最初希望记录核复杂体对社区造成的附带伤害——这种伤害由城乡不平等结构决定，乡村为东京的电力生产做出牺牲——却遇到了Hatsumi的质疑。如果说辐射的数值测量可能被利用，那么民族志研究同样如此。复述以伤害为中心的公共话语存在风险。后3.11日本的人类学家应该讲述什么故事？更广泛地说，科学知识生产（包括解析“变幻莫测的科学、政治、法律和媒体报道”的民族志知识）的利害关系是什么？Morimoto标题中的“核幽灵”是Hatsumi在其研究早期提出的概念，如同他早期的田野调查意识到自己在错误的原因下寻找错误的东西一样，这一概念贯穿全书。核幽灵概括了后3.11日本的经历：某种无形且可怕的东西被超视觉化（通过公共表征、辐射监测站、装满了受污染土壤的塑料袋、Morimoto自己的盖革计数器），从而遮蔽了人、生活方式和故事——Morimoto认为这些才是应当关注的适当对象。然而，我们不应忽视辐射的危险。对Morimoto的许多对话者来说，在家中与辐射共存、耕耘世代相传的土地，是过有意义的生活和安详死亡的条件。生态互相关联的“缘”网络将人与关系置于情境中。通过梳理围绕辐射暴露和去污的、常常自相矛盾的科学进展，Morimoto展示了“合理”暴露对不同的人意味着不同的事情，福祉必须被整体地理解。福岛的“灰色地带”既指地理上由不断变化的疏散区域指定（第三章）及同样变化着的决定居民补偿的政策（第四章）所标记的空间，也指围绕辐射短期和长期影响的认识论不确定性。政治决策（先于科学决定而非遵循科学决定）产生了南相马这个“分裂的社区”，其中“污染物不均地落在预先存在的社会、文化和政治边界上，居民在其中持续生活并以此重新定位后3.11世界”（52页）。对辐射话题的重新定位是策略性的、实用的和存在主义的。在一个关键段落中（137页），Morimoto描述了从持反核或反政府政治立场的人的角度来看，“TEPCO事故必须保持危险”；其他人则在维持政府对丢失和受损财产的特定补偿水平方面有利益，因此“TEPCO事故的污染必须被认为是不安全的”。对于像Morimoto年长的对话者那样希望回家“安详死亡”的人，“污染物的持续存在以及相关补偿是延长异化期的标志，必须结束。”（137页）不同的行动者需要从社会和科学共识中获得不同的东西，尽管共识没有达成。在缺乏共识的情况下，问题确实是：该怎么办——回家安全吗？——以及欲望（除了伤害之外）如何指导人们的行动。在此背景下，Morimoto的书探讨了“科学作为社会面对无形危害的主要方法的局限”（137页），这一取向在COVID-19大流行之后对许多人来说都很熟悉。这是一部厚重的民族志，我可以想象在医学人类学、环境人类学、科学技术研究和日本研究的本科生和研究生研讨班上教授其中的章节。我最喜欢的章节是那些更为聚焦的。例如，第五章“放射性蚊子和半衰期科学”将Morimoto在哥伦比亚大学参加辐射安全官员培训与福岛一位名叫坪仓博士的科学家的以辐射为主题的广播节目并置。安全官员培训的主题是将辐射暴露保持在“尽可能低的合理水平”（123页），同时，公众对辐射的担忧被表征为“不科学”和“恐惧驱动”（124页）。相比之下，坪仓博士理解人们获取本地特定数据的愿望。通过考虑本地生态和社会网络，他细致地关注居民如何做出明智的减少风险决策。Morimoto自己的信息与坪仓博士一致：虽然辐射确实有害，但还有其他可能更具破坏性的伤害——比如疏散带来的二次健康风险——国家或关于TEPCO事故的公共话语都没有充分关注这些。本书本可以更详细地讨论这些其他风险，给人的印象是，从人类学家的角度来看，对居民叙遗漏的忽略与任何健康影响一样具有破坏性。另一个精彩的章节是第九章“追逐野猪”，专注于国家在补救策略中对生态背景的忽视。事实证明，日本政府一直在将野猪从禁区赶走，却没有考虑野猪去了哪里。这一章美丽而悲剧地阐述了“去污在福岛沿海产生了一种伤害生态，使当地人、野猪、当地食物链和土地本身都沦为核废料生产的共犯”（216页）。野猪——愉快地栖息在被人类耕作干扰的土地上，吃人类通常采集的美味食物，并且通常是人类的食物来源——现在被猎杀，仅仅作为核废料被焚烧。这本“关于”后3.11福岛的书远远超出了其主题。Morimoto的发现与我最近与科罗拉多州博尔德县荒野-城市交界处一场毁灭性的当地火灾相关的作品有许多共鸣——在社区关于谁被视为合法“受害者”（4页）的分歧，以及失去家园与房屋虽完好但受到不确定污染（50页）哪种情况更糟糕的问题上。我与大气科学家关于通常通过技术科学测量可知的无形空气污染的合作，谈到了与Morimoto追踪的相同的可量化数据与主观经验之间的复杂关系，即定量“数据不一定验证或与个体的主观经验对话，有时数据可能否认它们”（134页）。Morimoto的书促使我们重新思考可见性与不可见性在感知和认知中的作用。技术科学进步长期以来使原本不可察觉的现象变得可见。核幽灵是否因为辐射不可见而真正更可怕（114页）？无形的东西也更容易被忽视，距离产生安全的幻觉。如同其他能源生产形式，“核能是一种产生并再生产可暴露社区的社会技术”，Morimoto提醒我们，“公共和政治话语[应当]关注暴露背后的个体故事和本地历史”（237页）。在北美背景下，环境正义社区的概念可能是一把双刃剑，因为以伤害为中心的叙述掩盖了人们可能对土地甚至对污染产业——通常是生计来源——的复杂情感。尽管强调了交叉性的、不成比例的危害，该概念也将这些社区与其他社区隔离开来。像Morimoto那样主张“我们都生活在同一个放射性世界”（234页）是有力量的。利害关系属于我们所有人。

title: Racial Excess: Black Labor and Media Technology in Salvador da Bahia, Brazil
abstract: Dominant narrators frame Salvador da Bahia, Brazil, as a premodern city of African culturalisms and harmonious race relations. This is supposedly the result of a benign colonial slavery. Using two composite stories about street vending and media technologies, this article moves outside of the Bahian frame and to its racial excess: the social, symbolic, and ideological scraps of Blackness that get cut out from dominant visual regimes of representation that cut across the past and the present. The article argues that to understand Black Bahians as modern participants, we must shift the relationship between Blackness and media from merely representation to that of technology and labor, namely, through media devices and platforms, in the informal economy. This shift grounds Blackness not as a matter of ethnicity and cultural identity but rather as one that works by and through racial capitalism and smart-city economies. The article ends by deconstructing the limits of hegemonic frames and working with excess as a means to comprise different representations of African diasporic communities who confront coloniality through their labor practices and racialized class positions.
title_zh: 种族过剩：巴西萨尔瓦多的黑人劳动与媒介技术
abstract_zh: 主流叙事将巴西巴伊亚州萨尔瓦多描绘成一座前现代的城市，充满非洲文化特色与和谐的种族关系。这被认为是良性殖民奴隶制的产物。通过两个关于街头贩卖和媒介技术的复合故事，本文跳出巴伊亚的框架，探讨其种族过剩：即过去和现在的视觉表征主导体制中被剔除的黑人身份的社会、符号和意识形态残余。文章认为，要理解黑人巴伊亚人作为现代参与者，必须将黑人性与媒介的关系从单纯的再现转向技术与劳动，即通过非正规经济中的媒介设备和平台。这种转变将黑人性不再视为种族和文化认同问题，而是种族资本主义和智慧城市经济运作的一部分。文章最后解构了霸权框架的局限，并将过剩作为一种手段，以构成面对殖民性的非洲散居社区的不同表征，这些社区通过其劳动实践和种族化的阶级地位来对抗殖民性。

title: Real Time in Rearview
abstract: This article explores what “real time” means to market actors by focusing on the traders, market designers, and engineers acting in the electricity markets of the United States. For these experts, real time is the time interval in which they cannot intervene using the instruments available to them. The advocates of real-time exchange attempt to insert more checkpoints into time previously left unaccounted for with the help of superior accounting methods and sensing technologies. In electricity markets, many drag the markets in the direction of real-time arrangements, where the trade interval skews ever closer to continuous; others, however, think that this trend is detrimental to the quality of both electricity production and market competition. I show that these divergences in opinion stem from the diversity of the technological worlds from which market actors come. I argue that experts’ economic imaginations and designs emerge in the thick of technological work, as afforded and constrained by the devices at their disposal, from electricity meters to digital spreadsheets to phase conductors. This article advances an agenda to think of contemporary capitalism from within the exigencies, affordances, and constraints provided by technological work cultures—from within a field I call techno-economics.
title_zh: 后视镜中的实时
abstract_zh: 本文通过关注在美国电力市场中活动的交易者、市场设计者和工程师，探讨“实时”对市场参与者意味着什么。对这些专家来说，实时是他们无法利用现有工具干预的时间间隔。实时交易所的倡导者试图借助更优越的会计方法和传感技术，在先前未被计入的时间点插入更多检查点。在电力市场中，许多人将市场推向实时安排的方向，交易间隔越来越接近连续；然而，另一些人认为这一趋势对电力生产和市场竞争的质量都有害。本文表明，这些意见分歧源于市场参与者来自不同的技术世界。作者认为，专家的经济想象和设计产生于技术工作的核心，受到他们可支配设备的支持与限制，从电表到电子表格再到相导线。本文提出一种议程，即从技术工作文化所提供的要求、可供性和限制出发思考当代资本主义——从一个我称之为技术经济学的领域出发。

title: Responsabilidad Social Empresarial, ritual y extractivismo

authors.name: Théo Milin
institutions: Équipe de Recherche Interlangue : Mémoires, Identités, Territoires

abstract: Lithium mining has engaged in different types of relations with Indigenous communities since arriving in the Salar de Atacama between the 1980s and 1990s. One such relations strategy, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), was deployed in several regions worldwide in the 1990s as a joint effort by the mining industry to improve its image and focus on the episteme of ‘sustainable mining.’ This research looks at Ayllu Wine and the Toconao Harvest Festival, organized by the winemakers’ cooperative and SQM, to analyze CSR in relation to the concepts of extractivism and ritual. On the basis of qualitative research using ethnographies, interviews, press archive reviews and secondary sources, this paper concludes that, in the midst of the current lithium boom, the Harvest Festival is, in spatial and temporal terms, a SQM governability strategy that produces tension in the community. Behind the festivity, discourse and iconography of ‘responsible mining’ lies booming extractivist production.
title_zh: 企业社会责任、仪式与采掘主义
abstract_zh: 自20世纪80年代至90年代锂矿开采进入阿塔卡马盐沼以来，其与土著社区的关系经历了不同阶段。其中一种关系策略——企业社会责任（CSR）——于20世纪90年代在全球多个地区部署，是采矿业为改善形象并聚焦于“可持续采矿”知识体系的一项联合努力。本研究关注由酿酒合作社和SQM公司组织的Ayllu Wine与托科瑙丰收节，以分析CSR与采掘主义和仪式概念的关联。基于使用民族志、访谈、新闻档案回顾和第二手资料的定性研究，本文得出结论：在当前锂矿繁荣期间，丰收节在时空上是一种SQM的治理策略，在社区中产生张力。在“负责任采矿”的庆典、话语和图像背后，是蓬勃发展的采掘主义生产。

title: Rolling in Modernity
journal_name: BIJDRAGEN TOT DE TAAL- LAND- EN VOLKENKUNDE
abstract: Abstract This article addresses the development of General Motors’ assembly plant in the port of Tanjung Priok in Batavia/Jakarta, Indonesia. The American multinational operated the plant—its first production line in Southeast Asia—between 1927 and 1955. General Motors gave impetus to Tanjung Priok’s economic importance, and it became a key element in the port’s ‘social-economic fabric’. Car manufacturing was considered a new phenomenon within the colonial economy of the Netherlands Indies, which had previously been largely agricultural/plantation-based. The company brought along new technologies and ways of organizing; it also advertised—for instance, via the company magazine GM World —the idea of free trade and actively tried to distinguish itself from the colonial establishment. However, this critical stance should not be overstated; as this article shows, General Motors was introducing alternative corporate perspectives and modern industrial elements in the Netherlands Indies but also became part of the Western colonial system.
title_zh: 滚动中的现代性
abstract_zh: 本文探讨了通用汽车在印度尼西亚巴达维亚/雅加达的丹戎不碌港组装厂的发展历程。这家美国跨国公司于1927年至1955年间运营该厂——其在东南亚的第一条生产线。通用汽车推动了丹戎不碌港经济重要性的提升，并成为该港“社会经济结构”的关键要素。在之前主要依赖农业/种植园的荷属东印度殖民经济中，汽车制造被视为一种新现象。该公司带来了新技术和组织方式；它还通过公司杂志《通用汽车世界》等渠道宣传自由贸易理念，并积极试图与殖民政权区分开来。然而，这种批判性立场不应被夸大；正如本文所示，通用汽车在荷属东印度引入了另类的企业视角和现代工业元素，但同时也成为西方殖民体系的一部分。

title: Solar streetlights in post-earthquake Nepal: Place, identity and gender in a displaced village
abstract: There is growing recognition of the benefits of providing displaced communities with accessible lighting systems, such as public streetlights. However, little anthropological research has been done on the impacts of lighting in displaced communities. In this article, I explore perceptions of the impacts of seven public solar streetlights on a displaced community’s sense of place attachment, identity, and gender relations in rural post-earthquake Nepal. There is demonstrable evidence that streetlights enhance safety and security. Less studied themes include the psychological impacts related to fear, social identity, sense of personal freedom, and place attachment. I argue that streetlight installation increases place attachment and facilitates the forming of new relationships with the socially constructed environment. I describe how respondents discuss the impact of streetlights on the daily rhythm of domestic chores and personal activities, and on their cultural beliefs and practices. The introduction of streetlights is associated with increased divisions between genders and generations, and inter-household jealousy. Increased attachment to the post-displacement environment could further deepen tensions and traumas associated with further displacement. More nuanced understanding of the impacts of streetlights, in addition to technical considerations, will improve provision for displaced and remote communities.
title_zh: 尼泊尔震后太阳能路灯：流离失所村庄中的地方、身份与性别
abstract_zh: 人们越来越认识到为流离失所社区提供可及的照明系统（如公共路灯）的好处。然而，关于照明对流离失所社区影响的人类学研究很少。在本文中，我探讨了七个公共太阳能路灯对尼泊尔农村震后流离失所社区的场所依恋感、身份认同和性别关系影响的感知。有证据表明路灯增强了安全性。较少研究的主题包括与恐惧、社会认同、个人自由感和场所依恋相关的心理影响。我认为路灯安装增加了场所依恋，并促进了与建构环境的新关系的形成。我描述了受访者如何讨论路灯对日常家务和个人活动节奏的影响，以及对其文化信仰和实践的影响。路灯的引入与性别和代际之间更大的分歧以及家庭间的嫉妒相关。对安置后环境的依恋增加可能加深与进一步流离失所相关的紧张和创伤。对路灯影响更为细致的理解，除了技术考虑，将改善对流离失所和偏远社区的供应。

title: Staying with the blackout: an insecure anthropology of energy
journal_name: JOURNAL OF THE ROYAL ANTHROPOLOGICAL INSTITUTE
abstract: Abstract In the twenty‐first century, blackouts have settled into a familiar sequence of events in the fully electrified world. After jolting publics into a sudden awareness of energy assemblages, they gradually disappear from public memory. This article is an exercise in dwelling on blackouts that have already begun to recede from public memory so as to better conceptualize ‘energy security’ as an object of anthropological critique. Examining expert reports and retrospective verbal accounts, I focus on the 2021 blackout of Texas and the 2015 nationwide blackout of Turkey. Drawing on my long‐term ethnographic work with the US electric grid, I punctuate these failures with an uneventful day at a high‐security operation building in New England. I show that the desire for security suffuses electricity assemblages, from secure buildings of operation, to governments securing passage for the electric current, to publics demanding uninterrupted electricity access. I argue that in grid experts’ imagination, energy futures hinge on securing high‐risk nodes while continually expanding grids so that potential failures might be better absorbed. This imagination, however, produces a false sense of security when contemporary threats to transmission are too wide‐ranging to isolate and will only be amplified by larger grids.
title_zh: 与停电共存：一种不安全的能源人类学
abstract_zh: 摘要 在二十一世纪，停电已成为完全电气化世界中一个熟悉的事件序列。在让公众突然意识到能源集合体之后，它们逐渐从公众记忆中消失。本文旨在深入探讨那些已经开始从公众记忆中消退的停电，以便更好地将“能源安全”概念化为人类学批判的对象。通过考察专家报告和回顾性的口头叙述，我重点关注了2021年德克萨斯州的停电和2015年土耳其全国范围的停电。结合我在美国电网的长期民族志工作，我将这些故障与新英格兰地区一个高安全运行大楼中平淡无奇的一天穿插讲述。我表明，对安全的渴望渗透在电力集合体中，从安全的运行大楼，到政府保障电流通行的安全，再到公众要求不间断的电力接入。我认为，在电网专家的想象中，能源的未来取决于保障高风险节点的安全，同时不断扩大电网，以便更好地吸收潜在的故障。然而，这种想象产生了一种虚假的安全感，因为当前对输电的威胁范围太广，无法孤立处理，而且只会被更大的电网放大。

title: Taiwanese Prehistory
abstract: In a previous Current Anthropology article considering the Scandinavian Bronze Age (Ling, Earle, and Kristiansen 2018), a model was proposed to explain the concentration of metal wealth and social stratification under conditions of low population density. This model is now considered to help understand anomalies in the archaeological sequence of eastern Taiwan during the Neolithic and Early Metal Ages. In contrast to Taiwan’s agriculturally richer western coast, evidence of complexity arose unexpectedly early on the east despite its more limited agricultural soils and lower populations. We propose that these outcomes resulted from a maritime economy, in which local agricultural surpluses finance distant voyaging that an emergent elite might control. Travels carried a substantial amount of rare nephrite from Taiwan’s eastern coast to Island Southeast Asia and the South China Sea. Subsequently, metals and glass technologies were introduced from there into Taiwan. This trade and technological transfer were earliest on the eastern coast, perhaps unexpected because it was more removed from the Chinese mainland, a likely source for cultural transfers. We propose that eastern coast Taiwanese populations developed an entrepreneurial raiding-trading political economy, perhaps involving slaves, that would explain these anomalies. Predating specialized merchant trading, a raiding-trading complex, not unlike later piracy, may have provided broadscale maritime interactions partially responsible for patterned developments of political complexity in this region of the world.
title_zh: 台湾史前史
abstract_zh: 在之前的一篇《当代人类学》文章中，考虑斯堪的纳维亚青铜时代（Ling, Earle, and Kristiansen 2018），提出了一个模型来解释在低人口密度条件下金属财富和社会分层集中的现象。现在，该模型被用来帮助理解台湾东部新石器时代和早期金属时代考古序列中的异常现象。与台湾农业更丰富的西海岸相比，东部的复杂性证据出乎意料地早出现，尽管其农业土壤有限且人口较少。我们认为，这些结果是海洋经济的产物，在这种经济中，当地的农业剩余资助了长途航行，而新兴精英可能控制这些航行。旅行携带了大量来自台湾东海岸的稀有软玉到东南亚岛屿和南海。随后，金属和玻璃技术从那里传入台湾。这种贸易和技术转移最早出现在东海岸，也许出乎意料，因为它远离中国大陆，而中国大陆可能是文化转移的来源。我们提出，台湾东海岸人口发展了一种企业家式的掠夺-贸易政治经济，可能涉及奴隶，这将解释这些异常现象。在专业商人贸易之前，一种掠夺-贸易复合体，类似于后来的海盗行为，可能提供了广阔的海洋互动，部分解释了这个世界区域政治复杂性模式化发展的原因。

title: The messy ethics of household biogas in Tanzania: ambivalence and aesthetics in energy‐from‐waste
journal_name: JOURNAL OF THE ROYAL ANTHROPOLOGICAL INSTITUTE
abstract: Abstract Household biogas is an off‐grid energy technology that converts human, animal, and agricultural waste into fuel. This article analyses the emergence and use of household biogas technologies in Tanzania to theorize energy ethics in a postcolonial world. It engages Jane Bennett's theorization of the ‘energetics’ and aestheticization of ethics to ask how people assert and think through their own notions of good energy in postcolonial Africa. It documents two distinct registers people use to evaluate the ethics of biogas. The ‘circle of life’ register mobilizes popular environmental aesthetics of circle, cycle, and reuse as well as neoliberal and socialist political aesthetics of self‐containment and self‐reliance to enchant biogas with an ethical aura. The ‘excremental ambivalence’ register, alternately, disenchants biogas through referencing the polyvalent semiotics of shit and the sedimentation of racial and economic inequalities that condition the propagation of biogas. People engage both registers in the context of specific political economic and ecological conditions that also affect biogas uptake or refusal. The article thus argues that political economy, materiality, and aestheticization all play a role in people's ethical orientation to biogas and that ambivalence is a defining feature of energy transition in the Global South.
title_zh: 坦桑尼亚家庭沼气的杂乱的伦理：废物能源中的矛盾与美学
abstract_zh: 摘要 家庭沼气是一种离网能源技术，将人类、动物和农业废物转化为燃料。本文分析了坦桑尼亚家庭沼气技术的出现和使用，以理论化后殖民世界中的能源伦理。它借鉴简·贝内特关于‘能量学’和伦理审美化的理论，探讨在后殖民非洲，人们如何主张和思考自己关于良好能源的观念。文章记录了人们用来评估沼气伦理的两种不同方式。‘生命循环’方式调动了流行的环境美学，如循环、循环和再利用，以及新自由主义和社会主义政治美学中的自足和自力更生，为沼气赋予了伦理光环。而‘排泄物矛盾’方式则通过提及粪便的多义符号学以及种族和经济不平等在沼气传播中的沉淀，从而解构了沼气的魅力。人们根据特定的政治经济和生态条件，同时使用这两种方式，这些条件也影响着沼气的采纳或拒绝。文章因此认为，政治经济、物质性和审美化都在人们对沼气的伦理取向中发挥作用，而矛盾是全球南方能源转型的一个显著特征。

title: The Role of Labour Market Intermediaries for Migrant Workers in Global Production Networks: The Example of Filipino Migrant Workers in the Taiwanese Semiconductor Industry
journal_name: GLOBAL NETWORKS-A JOURNAL OF TRANSNATIONAL AFFAIRS
abstract: ABSTRACT This article contributes to the literature at the intersection of migration and global production networks (GPNs) by examining the role of labour market intermediaries (LMIs) for migrant workers. It demonstrates mediation processes by LMIs and elaborates on migration networks in the global labour market through qualitative and quantitative data. It examines the role of LMIs in responding to mechanisms in GPN, including zero inventory and just‐in‐time production, and the impact of private employment agents on migrant workers, particularly on their career paths. The article found that LMIs play an active role in the mediation and cooperation between migrant labour and firms and in shaping structural conditions for migrant workers in response to global competitive pressures. However, LMIs play a controversial role in social upgrading. Private LMIs are identified as having a negative impact on career paths of migrant workers.
title_zh: 劳动力市场中介在全球生产网络中对移民工人的作用：以台湾半导体行业的菲律宾移民工人为例
abstract_zh: 摘要 本文通过考察劳动力市场中介（LMIs）对移民工人的作用，为移民与全球生产网络（GPNs）交叉领域的文献做出贡献。它展示了LMIs的调解过程，并通过定性和定量数据阐述了全球劳动力市场中的移民网络。本文考察了LMIs在应对GPN机制（包括零库存和准时生产）中的作用，以及私营就业机构对移民工人，特别是其职业道路的影响。文章发现，LMIs在移民劳工与企业之间的调解与合作中，以及在应对全球竞争压力塑造移民工人的结构性条件方面发挥着积极作用。然而，LMIs在社会提升方面扮演着有争议的角色。私营LMIs被确定对移民工人的职业道路产生负面影响。

title: Volumes
abstract: Recent years have witnessed the advancement of several technocratic interventions in the context of the global environmental crisis that aim to calculate and track different objects of environmental concern at various scales. In this article, I focus on how such technocratic interventions are transforming the processes by which tropical timber is technically rendered into calculational abstractions known as “volumes” in Peru’s tropical timber supply chains. Drawing on twenty-four months of fieldwork following the activities of loggers, timber industrialists, and state technocrats across Peru’s Amazonian region of Loreto, I show how calculational abstractions can never fully circumvent the frictions of power, history, and bodily experience. Rather, technocratic interventions aiming to standardize tropical timber-calculation procedures ultimately transform volumes into fertile ethnographic terrains from which to appreciate how competing forms of political imagination intersect and collide with each other as Amazonia enters the age of climate change and biodiversity loss. RESUMEN Durante los últimos años, distintas intervenciones tecnocráticas han sido desplegadas en el contexto de la crisis ambiental global con el fin de calcular y trazar distintos objetos de preocupación ambiental a distintas escalas. En este artículo, me centro en cómo estas intervenciones tecnocráticas están transformando los procesos por los cuales la madera tropical es convertida en abstracciones calculacionales llamadas “volúmenes” dentro de las cadenas de suministro de madera tropical del Perú. Sobre la base de veinticuatro meses de trabajo de campo siguiendo las actividades de madereros, industriales y tecnócratas del Estado en la región amazónica de Loreto, muestro cómo las abstracciones calculacionales nunca pueden escapar del todo de las fricciones del poder, la historia y la experiencia corporal. Más bien, las intervenciones tecnocráticas que buscan estandarizar los procedimientos de calculo sobre la madera tropical transforman los volúmenes en terrenos etnográficos fértiles desde los cuales es posible apreciar cómo distintas formas de imaginación política se intersectan y colisionan al tiempo que la Amazonía ingresa a la era del cambio climático y la perdida de biodiversidad.
title_zh: 体积
abstract_zh: 近年来，在全球环境危机的背景下，出现了若干技术官僚干预措施，旨在不同尺度上计算和追踪各种环境关注对象。本文聚焦于这些技术官僚干预如何改变了秘鲁热带木材供应链中将热带木材技术上转化为称为“体积”的计算抽象的过程。基于在秘鲁亚马逊洛雷托地区跟随伐木者、木材实业家和国家技术官僚活动进行的二十四个月田野调查，我展示了计算抽象永远无法完全规避权力、历史和身体经验的摩擦。相反，旨在标准化热带木材计算程序的技术官僚干预最终将体积转化为肥沃的民族志田野，从中可以领略到随着亚马逊进入气候变化和生物多样性丧失的时代，竞争性的政治想象形式如何相互交叉和碰撞。摘要：近年来，在全球环境危机的背景下，出现了若干技术官僚干预措施，旨在不同尺度上计算和追踪各种环境关注对象。本文聚焦于这些技术官僚干预如何改变了秘鲁热带木材供应链中将热带木材技术上转化为称为“体积”的计算抽象的过程。基于在秘鲁亚马逊洛雷托地区跟随伐木者、木材实业家和国家技术官僚活动进行的二十四个月田野调查，我展示了计算抽象永远无法完全规避权力、历史和身体经验的摩擦。相反，旨在标准化热带木材计算程序的技术官僚干预最终将体积转化为肥沃的民族志田野，从中可以领略到随着亚马逊进入气候变化和生物多样性丧失的时代，竞争性的政治想象形式如何相互交叉和碰撞。

title: “South-South” Capitalist Extractive Patriarchy

authors.name: Justin Lee Haruyama
institutions: University of British Columbia, Okanagan Campus

abstract: Much scholarly and popular ink has been spilled in debates regarding whether contemporary Chinese economic investments in Africa constitute a “New Chinese Empire.” Focusing on macrolevel politics and state-to-state relations, both sides of this debate tend to ignore the everyday lived realities of Chinese migrants and local Africans. In this article, based on two years of ethnographic fieldwork at Chinese-operated mining enterprises in rural Zambia, I analyze intersecting inequalities of class, race, and gender that structure intimate relationships between Zambian women and Chinese men. The constraints on women’s agency that emerge when such relationships end are enmeshed within the wider structural disparities between Zambia and China today. These disparities result as much from the institutional policies of the Chinese state and state-owned enterprises as they do from the behavior of individual Chinese men. Deconstructing official narratives, I demonstrate how these policies operate as a form of “South-South” capitalist extractive patriarchy.
title_zh: “南南”资本主义榨取性父权制
abstract_zh: 关于当代中国在非洲的经济投资是否构成“新中华帝国”的争论，学术界和大众媒体已经耗费了大量笔墨。聚焦于宏观政治和国家间关系，争论双方往往忽视了中国移民和当地非洲人的日常现实生活。本文基于在赞比亚农村中国运营的矿业企业进行的两年民族志田野调查，分析了阶层、种族和性别的交叉不平等如何构建了赞比亚女性与中国男性之间的亲密关系。此类关系结束时对女性能动性的限制，嵌入在当今赞比亚与中国之间更广泛的结构性差异中。这些差异既源于中国政府和国有企业的制度政策，也源于个体中国男性的行为。通过解构官方叙事，我展示了这些政策如何作为一种“南南”资本主义榨取性父权制运作。

title: “This place is fake:” green capitalism and the production of scarcity in Kigali, Rwanda
abstract: Abstract This article is about green capitalism, demolition, and the production of housing scarcity in Kigali, Rwanda. It follows Kiyovu cy'abakene—a real place that was near zero‐carbon, built with renewable resources, owned and operated by Kigali residents—as it was first reimagined as a rhetorical “slum” and then converted into an actual one by force. And it follows the design and construction of Batsinda Housing estate, a sustainable solution to a fictional “crisis” of inadequate housing in Kigali. Drawing on several years of ethnographic research, I argue that in Kigali, and many cities like it, the destruction of built environments is not only about local elites who wish to demolish “slums” or “informal settlements” to build “world‐class” luxury cities. The demolition of neighborhoods and the displacement of people who live there is also done in the service of making new markets for green commodities through the production of scarcity. To manufacture effective demand for green commodities while maintaining their monopoly over what constitutes “sustainable,” Kigali's international teams of managers and consultants must render alternative, ecologically sound, African‐owned neighborhoods and building technologies “unsustainable.”
title_zh: “这个地方是假的：”基加利（卢旺达）的绿色资本主义与稀缺性的生产
abstract_zh: 本文探讨绿色资本主义、拆迁以及基加利住房稀缺性的生产。它关注Kiyovu cy'abakene——一个真实存在的、近乎零碳、使用可再生资源建造、由基加利居民拥有和运营的地方——它首先被重新想象为一个修辞意义上的“贫民窟”，然后被迫转化为一个实际的贫民窟。文章还探讨了Batsinda住宅区的设计和建造，这是为基加利住房短缺的虚构“危机”提供的一个可持续解决方案。基于数年的民族志研究，我认为在基加利及许多类似城市，建成环境的破坏不仅关乎希望拆除“贫民窟”或“非正式定居点”以建设“世界级”豪华城市的地方精英。社区的拆除和居民的流离失所也是为了通过制造稀缺性来为绿色商品创造新市场。为了制造对绿色商品的有效需求，同时维持他们对“可持续”定义的垄断，基加利的国际管理者与顾问团队必须将替代性的、生态健全的、非洲人拥有的社区和建筑技术渲染为“不可持续”的。

title: An anthropology of impossible futures
abstract: This guest editorial explores the intricate relationship between anthropology and the concept of impossible futures, focusing on the global push towards electric vehicles (EVs) and the lithium energy assemblage. Drawing inspiration from a lecture by palaeobiologist Mark Williams, a member of the Anthropocene Working Group (AWG), the author reflects on the Anthropocene epoch and the human‐caused transformations of the earth. It examines the European Green Deal's impact on the automotive industry, the global struggle for lithium and the paradoxes of green technology investments. It questions the feasibility of the envisioned future, emphasizing the contradictions within global capitalism and the potential futility of climate change mitigation efforts. The author calls for a reorientation in anthropological research, focusing on novel forms of unity, solidarity, justice and interspecies bonds in the face of seemingly impossible conditions. It concludes with a contemplation of anthropology's role in translating and understanding social life in the context of unattainable futures without losing sight of the discipline's contested past and inherent hope.
title_zh: 不可能未来的人类学
abstract_zh: 这篇客座社论探讨了人类学与不可能未来概念之间的复杂关系，重点关注全球向电动汽车（EV）和锂能源集合体的推进。作者从古生物学家马克·威廉姆斯（人类世工作组成员）的一次演讲中汲取灵感，反思了人类世时代以及人类引起的地球转变。文章审视了欧洲绿色协议对汽车工业的影响、全球对锂的争夺以及绿色技术投资的悖论。它质疑了所设想的未来的可行性，强调了全球资本主义内部的矛盾以及气候变化缓解努力的潜在徒劳。作者呼吁在人类学研究中重新定位，关注在面对看似不可能的条件时的新形式的团结、正义和跨物种联系。最后，文章思考了人类学在无法实现的未来背景下翻译和理解社会生活中的作用，同时不失去该学科有争议的过去和固有的希望。

title: His Dark Materials Among the Displays, the Pitt Rivers Museum, December 12, 2022 to December 31, 2023
abstract: There she found herself outside a grand building, a real Oxford-looking building that didn't exist in her world at all, though it wouldn't have looked out of place … She discovered that it was a museum …. At the back of the great iron and glass hall was the entrance to another part … in this second chamber she found herself surrounded by things she knew well: there were showcases filled with Arctic clothing just like her own furs – with sledges and walrus ivory carvings and seal-hunting harpoons – with a thousand and one jumbled trophies and relics and objects of magic and tools and weapons, and not only from the Arctic, as she saw, but from every part of this world. Philip Pullman, The Subtle Knife, Chapter 4 In the fourth chapter of fantasy author Pullman's (1997) The Subtle Knife, Lyra, his young protagonist, stumbles upon the Pitt Rivers Museum while wandering in a parallel world. While this alternate Oxford proves strange to Lyra—full of people whose souls do not reside outside their bodies as talking animal companions—the Pitt Rivers, an institution that does not exist in her version of the city, feels familiar. A recent exhibition of props and costumes from the BBC/HBO television adaptation of Pullman's His Dark Materials series sees objects displayed across three Oxford museums in 2023—The History of Science Museum, the Story Museum, and the Pitt Rivers. Of these, the Pitt Rivers is the only one to appear in the novels and television program. The museum's inclusion in a fantasy series suggests that there exists a permeable boundary between the fantastical and the ethnographic. However, unlike the academic literature that critiques these ties, Pullman's works of fiction embrace an exotic take on the material culture of non-European and non-Euro-American peoples. While not a full exhibition, the display of objects from a fantasy series alongside ethnographic collections presents an opportunity to revisit critiques of the ethnographic museum form and to reconsider how such museums' many, varied publics approach ethnographic collections. Through a door at the back of the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, the Pitt Rivers appears to the casual museum goer to be an extension of the prior, as Lyra assumed. However, the transition from the Natural History Museum into the Pitt Rivers is a stark one. The main hall of the former is grand and full of natural light, the towering articulated dinosaur skeletons given ample space for visitors to admire them. By comparison, the Pitt Rivers appears to be a shadowed, crowded cavern of curiosities. Finding the cases that contain the props involves navigating a riot of glass boxes, packed with objects grouped, in keeping with the museum's mandate, by type. The Pitt Rivers website includes a map that shows the locations of the props, as well as other objects and exhibits linked to the Arctic. Set out in numbered order, the list leads guests on a set course through the museum, providing a brief description of each listed object along with simple questions for young visitors to answer. With eight stops total, the “His Dark Materials Self-guided Museum Trail” includes, Lyra's Northern coat, hat, and gloves; a seal intestine parka and cape; Mary Malone's I Ching box; the Amber Spyglass and seed pods; the Wandering in Other Worlds display; a display of snow goggles; Mrs Coulter's locket; and Ruta Skadi's armour, dress, and throwing nails. Much of the first novel in Pullman's series, Northern Lights—and the first season of the television program—takes place in a fantastical version of the Nordic Arctic. As someone whose research concerns perceptions of the Arctic, the inclusion of Arctic material culture in the museum's self-produced educational materials piqued my curiosity and served as the focus of my visit. Lyra's Northern clothing is the presumed highlight of the His Dark Materials display as the only set of objects associated with the series' main character. They are also the most compellingly displayed of the props. A mannequin wearing the coat stands in a case at a back corner of the ground floor, alongside gut parkas collected from Inuit and Unangax̂ communities. Several fur parkas fill an adjacent case. The tan prop coat with its long-haired lining does not immediately stand out from its surroundings. Even the red of the hat and gloves, positioned above the headless torso and attached to the sleeve ends, are complemented by a nearby photo of Greenlandic Inuit, the women in similarly bright red anoraks. The only indication that the mannequin in prop clothing is different from its companions is a blue text panel at its foot, describing the clothing and its role in the series. The next stop on the trail is a gut parka and cape, on display in the same case as the prop clothing. Despite there being no signage related to the His Dark Materials display accompanying the gut attire, these objects attracted more attention and interest from the dozen or so passers-by I observed on the day of my visit in the spring of 2023. Lack of familiarity with gut as a clothing material seemed to compel visitors to stop and examine. This pattern held for the other props. Few visitors appeared to take note of the out-of-place objects as they passed through the maze of display cases, leaving the added props to blend into the visual noise. Why, then, bother to exhibit them? The simple, pragmatic response is audience engagement—a desire to appeal to the young audience of the books and show. In addition to the map, the museum website provides additional information on the props, with a page dedicated to each. Some of these pages contain information on related permanent collection objects. The page on Lyra's coat notes the “indigenous [sic] ingenuity” of communities who use intestine for waterproof clothing. On other pages, information is limited to the use of the objects in the series. All pages include reflections from students who participated in museum education sessions centered on the props. The description of these sessions, meant to encourage students to “reflect on the literary themes and characters in Philip Pullman's novels,” suggest the exhibit's intended audience. Ethnographic museums and their collections exist in a continuous state of uncertainty. Museum professionals and museum audiences have proposed a variety of approaches to revitalizing, reforming, and reimagining such institutions (Janes & Sandell, 2019; Lilje & Clark, 2019; Macdonald, 2020, 2022). However, attracting audiences by including objects born of fantasy risks intensifying the sense of the exotic that ethnographic museums have tried to escape. Centering the fictional story of a White British girl raised in the upper class surrounds of a magical, alternate-reality Oxford reinforces the sense that the Pitt Rivers collections are themselves mystical artifacts of the strange and unknown. Even as the permanent signage in the parka display invokes the “ingenious ways of surviving” devised by Arctic peoples, it places those peoples and their ways of life at a distance. This distance comes into sharper focus when Lyra's coat and its owner are considered. Alongside the television costume, the beautiful hide and gut parkas reveal something of the colonial relations that assembled the ethnographic museum. Here, material culture continues to serve as a prop of the 19th century British colonial imagination, even as that imagination has come under increased scrutiny. That museums trade in fictions is not a new insight (MacDonald & Silverstone, 1990). Oxford too, is a purveyor of fantasy. Pullman's writing illustrates this well. His home for decades, Pullman's magic-laden Oxford is the product of fond familiarity. Both city and university play a primary role in his series. The complex matrix of power and wealth that undergird the city-university blur into the magic of Pullman's world, where they remain uncritiqued. For its part, the Pitt Rivers of His Dark Materials conveys a treasure-trove-like wonder, the product of the author's consumption and reproduction of the museum's fictions. Those who study the North have commented on the fictions tied to the region, noting its mythologization as a realm of adventure and magic (Bravo, 2019; Davidson, 2005; Powell, 2007). In the popular narratives of the professional explorers of the 19th and 20th centuries, Inuit and other Northern peoples appear as friendly assistants, or else as extensions of the natural environment (Peary, 1910; Stefánsson, 1913). While the television show largely skirts the inclusion of Northern peoples, the magical North of the His Dark Materials novels does not avoid them entirely. While unnamed on screen, self-identified “Samoyeds” kidnap Lyra and bring her to the research facilities of the villainous Magisterium in Northern Lights (Pullman, 1995: 236). Additionally, despite its real-world distance from communities that make such garments, Lyra acquires a gut parka in the Nordic Arctic of her world (Pullman, 1995: 177). One such parka is worn, without comment, by one of her on-screen captors. Other Northern peoples also appear. The men who patrol the research base at fictional Bolvangar are described as “Tartars” in the books, presumably based on real-world Tatar peoples. The fictional Tartars, although largely antagonistic, are not always so. One ally, a British man thought lost on an Arctic expedition, is made a shaman by Tartars in Lyra's Siberia, giving him supernatural powers (Pullman, 1997). That the technologies of Northern peoples are freely available to Lyra and her friends—in one case through the medium of a White male “expert” in traditional spirituality—is in keeping with Arctic exploration narratives of the past. In His Dark Materials, these tropes are taken further, as the relevant tools are accessible to the protagonists without the bother of interpersonal relations with Northern communities of origin. The series' depiction of the Arctic as a realm of exploration and heroic endeavor is perhaps a better fit at both the History of Science Museum and the Story Museum, where relations to the real peoples of the region are more easily overlooked. The former has a separate exhibition space for what it calls Lyra's Worlds. There, a prop alethiometer—the tool Lyra uses to communicate with Dust, the novels' sentient dark matter—shares a case with real-world scientific tools. Sixteenth and 17th century handheld astronomical instruments are shown to be quite like the imaginary device. Together, the objects tell a simple story of the power of scientific inquiry, in both our world and Lyra's. The Story Museum has an even clearer path forward, having added the Subtle Knife—a blade used to cut between parallel worlds—and other television props to a case dedicated to Philip Pullman. These fit well among the other interactive exhibits dedicated to children's fantasy tales and their authors. The Pitt Rivers Museum is an institution that has grappled creatively and purposefully with its origins. No longer the personal collection of a colonial officer, over several decades it has worked with communities of origin, local stakeholders, and artists from around the world on many projects. Recent efforts, as I encountered them, work to mixed effect. A television showing Serbian performance artist Marina Abramović caressing, recoiling from, and gesturing at a variety of objects from the collections elicited chuckles from teenagers on a school trip. The spectacle of Abramović—a White woman—encountering objects predominantly from non-European cultures makes an uncomfortable addition to the museum's ground floor. However, in a side gallery, the special exhibition Unmasked: Spirit in the City uses an art installation to explore a popular form of African masquerade with exceptional creativity and care. Taken together, the two demonstrate both the pitfalls and the strengths of engaging creatively with ethnographic materials. The Wandering in Other Worlds exhibit, listed as the fifth stop on the His Dark Materials trail, occupies a single case. Like Unmasked, Other Worlds was co-created with members of the community it describes, the Evenki of Siberia. The resulting display takes seriously the task of explaining Evenki cosmology to a presumed non-Evenki audience. Having taken in that exhibit, I left the Pitt Rivers hopeful. At their best, ethnographic museums can provide platforms for sharing complex stories, told from myriad perspectives and drawn from our own multifarious world(s). This project has received funding from the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program (Grant Agreement number: 724317—ARCTIC CULT—ERC-2016-COG).
title_zh: 黑暗物质在展品中：皮特·里弗斯博物馆，2022年12月12日至2023年12月31日
abstract_zh: 在菲利普·普尔曼的《黑暗物质》系列中，年轻主角莱拉偶然发现了皮特·里弗斯博物馆。2023年，该博物馆与牛津其他两家博物馆合作举办了BBC/HBO电视剧版《黑暗物质》的道具和服装展览。本文考察了该展览如何将虚构物品与民族志收藏并置，揭示了博物馆展示中幻想与异国情调之间的张力。展览中的道具，如莱拉的北极外套，与因纽特人和尤皮克人的肠衣大衣并排放置，强调了殖民关系和北方地区的虚构化。文章反思了民族志博物馆面临的挑战，即如何在吸引观众的同时避免强化异域感。作者呼吁对博物馆的叙事和权力结构进行批判性审视。

title: Kamapim gutpela man: Papua New Guinean and Chinese refinery workers' changing understandings of becoming a good man
abstract: ABSTRACT This article adds to research on emerging masculinities in the Pacific by analysing how Papua New Guinean and Chinese male employees' intercultural work experiences impact their perceptions of becoming a good man. The idea of a good man acts as a benchmark for assessing the adaptability of Papua New Guinean employees to new work environments and determining if Chinese colleagues are their desired partners. I illustrate this point by first considering ‘becoming’ as an alternate framework to the binary framework reflected in earlier research. I next describe how Papua New Guinean workers impress their Chinese supervisors through negotiations and concessions about industrial and subsistence farming time, as well as how working with Papua New Guinean workers alters Chinese employees' perceptions of work. Finally, I demonstrate how employment practices foster Papua New Guinean workers' evolving perspectives on becoming a gutpela man (‘good man’) and Chinese employees' evolving perspectives on becoming a good person, a vital route to becoming a chenggong man (‘successful man’). This article proposes characterizing emerging masculinities as hybrid identities that are context‐dependent, interculturally exchanged and temporal by presenting two parties' new thoughts on becoming a good man. This article demonstrates modulatory power dynamics in the Chinese refinery based on a two‐way narrative as opposed to portraying Chinese management as the dominating force.
title_zh: 《成为好男人》：巴布亚新几内亚和中国炼油厂工人对成为好男人理解的变化
abstract_zh: 本文通过分析巴布亚新几内亚和中国男性员工跨文化工作经验如何影响他们对成为好男人的看法，为太平洋地区新兴男性气质研究增添了内容。好男人的观念是评估巴布亚新几内亚员工适应新工作环境的能力以及判断中国同事是否是理想合作伙伴的基准。我通过首先将“成为”视为替代早期研究中二元框架的另一种框架来说明这一点。接下来，我描述了巴布亚新几内亚工人如何通过关于工业与生存农业时间的谈判和让步给中国主管留下深刻印象，以及与中国工人合作如何改变中国员工对工作的看法。最后，我展示了雇佣实践如何促进巴布亚新几内亚工人对成为gutpela man（“好男人”）的不断演变的观点，以及中国员工对成为好人（成为chenggong man（“成功男人”）的重要途径）的不断演变的观点。本文通过呈现双方对成为好男人的新思考，提出将新兴男性气质描述为依赖于情境、跨文化交流和暂时的混合身份。本文展示了基于双向叙事的中国炼油厂中的调节性权力动态，而不是将中国管理层描绘为主导力量。

title: A Feast of Flowers: Race, Labor, and Postcolonial Capitalism in Ecuador By ChristopherKrupa. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2022. 318 pp.
abstract: “At what moment was this idea lost? At what moment does such ordinary, everyday beauty become a luxury?” –Jamaica Kincaid (2001) Cayambe is a small city located in the northern Ecuadorian Andes with a population of around 40,000 inhabitants. It is on the main Pan-American Highway and therefore easily reachable by car or local transportation. It has a long-standing Indigenous heritage, including one of the largest pyramids or “tolas,” called Puntiachil, a bit eroded but still largely visible within the city limits. However, at this point most of its inhabitants are mestizos, with the larger Indigenous rural population living in its surrounding area. When one first visits the city of Cayambe, one is struck by many things, including its deceiving sleepy-town persona, a dynamic presence of Indigenous heritage (nowadays the main streets have their names in both Spanish and Kichwa), and the surrounding flower plantations that have marked its development since the mid-1990s. However, one would never intimate the central place the city occupies in the postcolonial landscape of our globalized world, and particularly how Cayambe is responding to very old “local/global” (see Hall, 1997) histories of capitalist processes while at the same embodying quite new ones expressed in postcolonial trappings. It is precisely credit to Krupa's work and this book that we are privy to the fact that there is more in Cayambe than would seem to meet the eye. Under those shimmery metallic rooftops that cover the greenhouses in the nearby mountainous landscape of Cayambe, there is a long-standing capitalist living history of colonialism and accumulation continuing to exploit the neighboring Indigenous and now the mestizo population. The book is based on three years of ethnographic work carried out in Cayambe and the Ecuadorian Andes between 2001–2015, and on previous on-and-off contact with the surrounding Indigenous communities since 1994. The book is structured into four sections of (more or less) equal page numbers, as well as an introduction and a very short conclusion. The introduction sets out the theoretical and ethnographic narrative of the book, expressing quite clearly that it “approaches capitalism as an object of ethnographic inquiry, focusing specifically on the genesis, establishment, and expansionary work of Ecuador's cut-flower sector in the Cayambe highlands, from the mid-1980s to the early twenty-first century” (p. 5). As Krupa states, his goal is “to understand the historically specific processes attending to rural capitalization in the postcolonial context and to theorize from those processes a South-centered understanding of late twentieth-century capitalist globalization” (p. 5). Each of the four sections develops this ongoing capitalist history from the more theoretical and general elements to the more local and ethnographic ones. However, this does not mean that the two, theory and ethnography, are not consistently intertwined as much as that the varying emphasis placed on these two elements serves as one of the continuing threads through which the local production history of flower production in Cayambe is told. At the same time, through the narrative, we are continuously able to marvel at the incredibly large global forces at work in Cayambe. These are the same forces that are met with enormous pride and courage from the standpoint of workers and the Indigenous population, since the northern Andes has also been one of the stalwarts of the Indigenous movement in Ecuador, and places like Cayambe have been at the vanguard of national Indigenous politics. Krupa also elaborates on a series of elements and issues that I think are welcome insights into a more contemporary understanding of postcolonial capitalism. One of them is the understanding of diversity and difference in this new global capitalist postcolonial landscape. Unlike its historical past, the postcolonial processes of capitalism no longer shy away from difference. Quite the contrary: “the interplay of diversity and inequality [might] be central to contemporary capitalism—rather than a distraction” (p. 9). Of course, in this rural Andean landscape, difference is marked racially and projected upon the Indigenous communities that continue to suffer the economic exploitation and cultural oppression that their ancestors did. However, Krupa emphasizes how this idea of the indio as a problem, a categorization shared by all oppressed minority groups, is a projection of the white/mestizo elite's own sense of guilt and foreboding. In this manner, he examines how the Ecuadorian racial elite has elaborated complex psychological “interiorizations” into the Indigenous psyche that say more about themselves in this postcolonial setting than it does about their supposed racialized subject of study. Krupa returns to this insight in his conclusion, using an Ecuadorian analysis of the “Indigenous question” written in the mid-1940s to impress upon us how this narrative of the Indigenous in need of saving and redemption has been reworked into the supposed more human desire (and nostalgia) of postcolonial capitalism. It is, we are asked to believe, contemporary engaged humane labor that will free the racial oppression binding Indigenous brethren, all the while looking to erase how those bondages were the products and artifacts of capitalist history themselves. Therefore, if the colonization of oppressed people meant seeing them as a problem, then supposedly “the history of post-colonial capitalism in Ecuador could be written as the quest to solve it” (p. 289). This is also precisely why Krupa wants Kincaid's tone “to haunt” his own (p. 8). And in doing so, I believe Krupa's work provides a much-needed roadmap of the uncanny way in which postcolonial capitalism seeks to erase centuries of exploitation while it pretends to present itself as a new/old (see Hall, 1997) form of humane development. This book is a welcome contribution to the local/global understanding of postcolonial development, one in which the Indigenous subject is much more aware of the fragility of our times.
title_zh: 鲜花盛宴：厄瓜多尔的种族、劳动与后殖民资本主义
abstract_zh: 被标记为书评摘要，但主要涉及花卉种植产业，与消费电子硬件无直接关联。

title: Asylum and extraction in the Republic of Nauru By Julia CarolineMorris. Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 2023. 318 pp.
abstract: Asylum and Extraction in the Republic of Nauru, by Julia Caroline Morris, is a detailed analysis of asylum processing in Nauru—a small island republic 2,046 miles northeast of the northern tip of Queensland, Australia, which has yet to be the subject of sustained ethnographic and historical research. Drawing on multisited ethnographic fieldwork and archival analysis in Nauru, Australia, and Geneva from 2014 to 2016, Morris offers an unprecedented look at how offshore detention functions as a global industry that has come to organize the everyday lives of local Nauruans. Morris treats detention as one node in an assemblage that deters refugees from entering Australia. A range of actors participate in this assemblage: private security firms, the Australian Border Force, and the Australian Department of Immigration and Border Protection, as well as NGO workers, journalists, and activists seeking to document human rights abuses. As some readers might know, the Australian government has historically used Nauru to incarcerate asylum seekers who attempted to arrive to Australian shores by boat. This first took place from 2001 to 2008, and again from 2013 to 2016, when people began arriving mainly from the following countries: Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka, Somalia, Bangladesh, and Pakistan. The second instance was distinct in that the government vowed that no asylum seekers who came by boat (labeled as “unauthorized maritime arrivals”) would be resettled in Australia. The Australian state poured billions of dollars into ensuring that the refugees stayed put on Nauru and gave up the very idea of Australia. And yet Nauru's marketing as a site of permanent resettlement has a much deeper history, one that goes back to Australian colonial exploits. Such infrastructures of extraction have set the precedent for Nauru's more recent carceral landscape, and this constitutes the book's core focus. The first half of the book traces the transformation of Nauru from a phosphate mining company town to a refugee detention company town, with detailed focus on the built environment and the relationship between local people, space, and the land. The second half of the book lays out the interests of the many stakeholders, from private security firms to Australian refugee resettlement workers to humanitarian organizations, who make up the offshore asylum industry. The central argument that organizes the book is that today's offshore asylum processes in Nauru share parallels and continuities with Australian state-led phosphate mining projects on the island in the early to mid-20th century. Morris writes that “extractive operations converge on the lives of minority populations.” Like phosphate, refugees also undergo a process of “extractive metallurgy,” which refers to the process of removing valuable raw metals from an ore and cultivating them into a purer form, without contaminants. Just as phosphate rock was subject to product testing, processes to verify “genuine” refugee claims are also subject to quality testing. By undergoing a barrage of medical tests, credible threat assessments, and other “fitness to travel” assessments (pp. 85–86), refugees also experience “refining” and “purification” processes, thus producing distinctions between “true refugees” and economic migrants. Here, more ethnographic detail on how asylum processes worked in practice would have strengthened this claim. This is worth mentioning because the book begins with the chemical equation for phosphate rock and sulfuric acid, which produces “superphosphate,” a fertilizer. This is followed by the 1951 Geneva Convention's definition of the refugee, implying that refugees and phosphate are treated in similar ways. While this is theoretically compelling, the reader wonders if it is necessary to analogize refugees to phosphate and refugee processing to phosphate mining in order to illustrate that refugees are being dehumanized in Nauru. While the book effectively shows that the phosphate industry has set the infrastructural precedents of the refugee-processing industry, this claim would have been supported by more elaboration on who in the offshore asylum assemblage is mobilizing this analogy. The book's strengths lie in its extraordinary historical and legal analysis of the mining agreements between the British Phosphate Commission (BPC) and the Nauruan government, as well as the mining industry's effects on Nauruan identity. Morris brilliantly lays out how phosphate is a “cultural identity” for Nauruans who took what was used as a colonial exploit and turned it into a source of economic independence. For this reason, phosphate is a symbol of both toxicity and self-governance, a marker of dispossession and decolonization depending on the historical period. And yet the Nauru Rehabilitation Corporation's takeover of phosphate mining, which was designed to rehabilitate several hectares of land destroyed by BPC mining in the 1960s, did little to revitalize things. This history, combined with powerful narratives of locals who have had to confront the consequences of the phosphate industry, such as chronic bronchitis and bodily injuries, show the devastating effects yet ongoing pull of phosphate on the island. This analysis marks an important moment in the study of a distinctly Australian brand of migrant deterrence, one that uses resource-poor islands to outsource the violence of border control. And yet as Morris shows, the Australian state is everywhere in Nauru even as it seeks to render itself invisible in the psyche of refugees. This book will undoubtedly activate new horizons of inquiry, including how the Australian state imagined Nauru as part of a larger “enforcement archipelago” (Mountz, 2011) in relation to Manus Island and Christmas Island, and the economic and cultural life of other similarly situated prison towns throughout the world. This book will be of interest to interdisciplinary scholars and anthropologists who study asylum, the production of migrant illegality in colonial settings, the social life of commodities, and labor and infrastructure. In sum, this book will leave a profound impact on readers, compelling them to think more critically about the question: For whom do refugees matter and why?
title_zh: 瑙鲁共和国的庇护与资源开采
abstract_zh: 《瑙鲁共和国的庇护与资源开采》由朱莉娅·卡罗琳·莫里斯撰写，深入分析了瑙鲁的庇护处理程序。瑙鲁是一个小岛共和国，位于澳大利亚昆士兰北部顶端东北方向2046英里处，此前尚未成为持续的民族志和历史研究对象。莫里斯利用2014年至2016年在瑙鲁、澳大利亚和日内瓦进行的多地点民族志田野调查和档案分析，提供了关于离岸拘留如何作为一个全球产业运作、并已组织起当地瑙鲁人日常生活的前所未有的视角。莫里斯将拘留视为一个阻止难民进入澳大利亚的集合体中的节点。多种行为者参与其中：私营安保公司、澳大利亚边境部队、澳大利亚移民和边境保护部，以及旨在记录人权侵犯的非政府组织工作人员、记者和活动家。正如一些读者所知，澳大利亚政府历史上曾利用瑙鲁监禁试图乘船抵达澳大利亚海岸的寻求庇护者。这首先发生在2001年至2008年，然后在2013年至2016年再次发生，当时人们主要来自伊朗、伊拉克、阿富汗、斯里兰卡、索马里、孟加拉国和巴基斯坦。第二次情况的不同之处在于，政府发誓不会将任何乘船前来的寻求庇护者（被称为“未经授权的海上抵达者”）重新安置在澳大利亚。澳大利亚政府投入了数十亿美元，确保难民留在瑙鲁，并放弃前往澳大利亚的想法。然而，瑙鲁作为永久重新安置地点的营销有着更深远的历史，可以追溯到澳大利亚的殖民剥削。这种开采基础设施为瑙鲁近期的监狱景观奠定了基础，这也是该书的核心焦点。书的前半部分追溯了瑙鲁从一个磷酸盐矿城镇转变为难民拘留公司城镇的过程，重点关注建筑环境以及当地人、空间和土地之间的关系。后半部分阐述了构成离岸庇护产业的众多利益相关者，从私营安保公司到澳大利亚难民重新安置工作人员，再到人道主义组织。该书的核心论点是，今天在瑙鲁的离岸庇护程序与20世纪早期至中期澳大利亚国家主导的岛上磷酸盐开采项目存在相似性和连续性。莫里斯写道，“开采行动汇聚在少数群体的生活中”。像磷酸盐一样，难民也经历了一种“提取冶金”过程，指从矿石中提取有价值的粗金属并将其培育成更纯净形式的过程。正如磷酸盐岩石经过产品测试一样，验证“真正”难民身份的过程也经过质量测试。通过接受一系列医疗测试、可信威胁评估和其他“旅行适宜性”评估（第85-86页），难民也经历了“精炼”和“净化”过程，从而区分“真正难民”和经济移民。在此，更多关于庇护程序实际运作的民族志细节会增强这一主张。值得注意的是，该书以磷酸盐岩石和硫酸的化学方程式开头，产生一种肥料“过磷酸钙”，随后是1951年《日内瓦公约》对难民的界定，暗示难民和磷酸盐以类似方式被对待。虽然这在理论上引人注目，但读者想知道是否有必要将难民类比为磷酸盐，将难民处理类比为磷酸盐开采，以说明难民在瑙鲁被非人化。尽管该书有效展示了磷酸盐工业为难民处理工业奠定了基础设施先例，但这一主张需要更多关于离岸庇护集合体中谁在运用这一类比的支持。该书的优势在于其对英国磷酸盐委员会与瑙鲁政府之间的采矿协议以及采矿业对瑙鲁身份影响的非凡历史和法理分析。莫里斯精彩地阐述了磷酸盐如何成为瑙鲁人的“文化身份”，他们将曾经作为殖民剥削的东西转化为经济独立的来源。因此，磷酸盐既是毒性的象征，也是自治的象征，根据历史时期不同，它既是剥夺的标志，也是非殖民化的标志。然而，瑙鲁康复公司接管磷酸盐开采，旨在恢复1960年代被英国磷酸盐委员会开采破坏的几公顷土地，但并未能重振局面。这段历史，加上当地人不得不面对磷酸盐产业后果（如慢性支气管炎和身体伤害）的有力叙述，展示了磷酸盐对岛上持续的影响和破坏性后果。这一分析标志着对一种独特的澳大利亚式移民威慑策略的重要研究，该策略利用资源匮乏的岛屿将边境控制的暴力外包。然而，正如莫里斯所展示的，澳大利亚国家在瑙鲁无处不在，尽管它试图在难民心理中隐匿自己。这本书无疑将开启新的研究视野，包括澳大利亚国家如何将瑙鲁视为与马努斯岛和圣诞岛相关的更大“执法群岛”的一部分，以及世界各地其他类似监狱城镇的经济和文化生活。这本书将吸引研究庇护、殖民环境下移民非法性的产生、商品的社会生活以及劳动和基础设施的跨学科学者和人类学家。总之，这本书将给读者留下深刻印象，促使他们更批判性地思考一个问题：难民对谁重要，为什么？

title: Bumpy Roads, Dusty Air: Gadbad and the Sensate Ecologies of Driving Work in Contemporary Mumbai
abstract: I decouple the commonly discussed ecological destruction and unsustainability wrought by cars from a discussion of what life lived and sustained around automobiles looks like. Through fieldwork with hereditary Muslim taxi drivers in Mumbai, I look at urban ecological relations with those who work in what I call sensate ecologies. A sensate-ecologies approach connects labor and urban ecology and argues for a collective rather than an individual subject of urban theory. What I describe here as drivers’ sensate ecological relations with a difficult city—a condition that is usually considered ecologically and infrastructurally unsustainable—calls into question assumptions about ecological damage and precarious urban life. By analyzing taxi driving as relational, sensate work. rather than as precarious labor, I argue that urban sensate ecologies produce expertise for hereditary drivers that sustain over generations. I conclude that even unsustainable ecological onslaughts of automobility produce coexistence and sustainable social and sensate relations.
title_zh: 颠簸道路，尘埃空气：当代孟买驾驶工作中的障碍与感官生态
abstract_zh: 我将通常讨论的汽车造成的生态破坏和不可持续性与围绕汽车所维持的生活分开。通过对孟买的世袭穆斯林出租车司机的田野调查，我审视了那些在我所谓的感官生态中工作的人与城市生态的关系。感官生态方法将劳动与城市生态联系起来，并主张城市理论的一个集体主体而非个体主体。我在此描述的司机与一个艰难城市的感官生态关系——一种通常被认为在生态和基础设施上不可持续的状况——质疑了关于生态破坏和 precarious 城市生活的假设。通过将出租车驾驶分析为关系的、感官的工作，而非 precarious 劳动，我认为城市感官生态为世袭司机产生了代代相传的专业知识。我得出结论，即使是汽车流动性不可持续的生态冲击也产生了共存和可持续的社会与感官关系。

title: Ecologies of quantification in waste management: Landfilling, e-waste recycling, and car breaking

authors.name: Daniel Sosna
institutions: Czech Academy of Sciences, Institute of Ethnology

authors.name: Barbora Stehlíková
institutions: Czech Academy of Sciences, Institute of Ethnology

authors.name: Pavel Mašek
institutions: Czech Academy of Sciences, Institute of Ethnology
University of West Bohemia in Pilsen

abstract: Quantification has become a privileged form of knowing and vehicle of governance. Anthropological critique has demonstrated that a view of numbers as independent carriers of meaning is untenable; instead, numbers should be conceptualized as being part of relations and temporalities, opening space for shifts in understanding. Proposing the perspective of ‘ecologies of quantification’, we acknowledge the wider notion of ecology that accommodates materiality, cognition, and experience, and acknowledges that the constituents of the relations are always in a process of becoming. We put waste management at the centre of our interest to explore the ways quantification attempts to conquer arguably one of the unruliest domains of contemporary social life. Based on our collaborative ethnographic research on the management of municipal solid waste, discarded electrical and electronic devices, and junked cars in Czechia, we point to problems emerging when numbers become stripped of their relations. Our research sheds light on experience in the process of quantification and demonstrates that there are multiple ways to know quantity.
title_zh: 垃圾管理中的量化生态：填埋、电子废物回收与汽车拆解
abstract_zh: 量化已成为一种特权的认知形式和管理工具。人类学批判表明，将数字视为独立的意义载体这一观点站不住脚；相反，数字应被概念化为关系和时间性的一部分，为理解上的转变开辟空间。通过提出“量化生态”的视角，我们承认更广泛的生态概念，它容纳了物质性、认知和经验，并承认关系的构成要素始终处于生成过程中。我们将垃圾管理置于兴趣中心，探索量化试图征服当代社会生活中最难以驾驭的领域之一的方式。基于我们在捷克对城市固体废物、废弃电子电气设备和报废汽车管理的合作民族志研究，我们指出了当数字脱离其关系时出现的问题。我们的研究揭示了量化过程中的经验，并表明存在多种认识数量的方式。

title: Ethnographies of Power: A Political Anthropology of Energy, de Tristan Loloum, Simone Abram y Nathalie Ortar
abstract: El vasto conjunto de infraestructuras que sostienen nuestra vida material parece asentarse cada vez con más frecuencia en un principio de invisibilidad. Desde el alcantarillado municipal hasta las conexiones en las que se basan nuestros dispositivos electrónicos, todas ellas tienden a desaparecer en túneles subterráneos o a desvanecerse bajo la forma de ondas intangibles. Si bien responde en ocasiones a criterios de salud, seguridad o comodidad, este deseo por ocultar las redes que tejen nuestra vida cotidiana tiene numerosas e importantes consecuencias políticas, en la medida en la que naturaliza procesos tan complejos como los que esconde, por ejemplo, el gesto de abrir o cerrar un grifo. En el caso concreto de las infraestructuras energéticas, este encubrimiento afecta tanto a los canales de distribución como a las propias fuentes de energía, que se establecen comúnmente en regiones periféricas y alejadas de los centros de poder. En los diferentes capítulos que componen Ethnographies of Power: A Political Anthropology of Energy, sus autoras reivindican la «repolitización» de la energía a través de un conjunto de investigaciones etnográficas, con las cuales se pretende desvelar aquello que hay detrás de las infraestructuras energéticas.
title_zh: 权力的民族志：能源的政治人类学
abstract_zh: 支撑我们物质生活的庞大基础设施似乎越来越频繁地建立在不可见性的原则上。从市政下水道到我们电子设备所依赖的连接，它们都倾向于消失在隧道中或化为无形的电波。虽然有时出于健康、安全或舒适的标准，但这种隐藏我们日常生活网络的行为具有许多重要的政治后果，因为它使得诸如打开或关闭水龙头这样复杂的自然化过程变得复杂。在能源基础设施的具体案例中，这种隐藏既影响分配渠道也影响能源本身，这些能源通常位于外围地区，远离权力中心。在《权力的民族志：能源的政治人类学》的不同章节中，作者们通过一系列民族志研究来倡导能源的“再政治化”，旨在揭示能源基础设施背后的事物。

title: Internet as an ideology: nationalistic discourses, and multiple subject positions of Chinese internet workers
abstract: Ideology works. This article examines how the Internet as a capital actor has become a nationalist ideology in China. Disclosing how nationalism serves to facilitate the expansion of China-based Internet platforms in the age of informational capitalism, we directly confront the Chinese Internet as an ideology apparatus that works to fulfill a dual logic of capital and territorial power. This article contributes to the study of three types of Chinese Internet workers: programmers, white-collar employees (excluding programmers), and assembly-line workers, and focuses on how nationalist discourses are created, which enthrall but at the same time are questioned by different workers who help fabricate nationalism as well as challenge it. We conceptualize topos of threat and referential strategy of collectivization as cultural and media tactics, driven by the nationalistic sentiments that form part of the “common sense” of Chinese users.
